es.summary: Lesión erosiva de la mucosa gástrica o duodenal causada principalmente por H. pylori o por AINE crónicos.
key_points: Dolor epigástrico que empeora entre comidas y mejora con alimentos o antiácidos.
H. pylori y AINE son los factores de riesgo más frecuentes.
Diagnóstico: prueba de aliento/serología/hemocultivo y endoscopia con biopsia.
Tratamiento: inhibidores de la bomba de protones + terapia antibiótica si hay H. pylori.
Complicaciones: sangrado gastrointestinal, perforación y obstrucción.

pathophysiology: El ácido gástrico daña la mucosa cuando la barrera protectora está comprometida.
H. pylori produce ureasa que neutraliza el ácido y genera inflamación crónica.
Los AINE inhiben la prostaglandina, reduciendo la secreción de moco y flujo sanguíneo mucosal.
risk_factors: Tabaquismo y consumo excesivo de alcohol.
Estrés crónico y antecedentes familiares de úlcera.
signs_symptoms: Dolor ardiente epigástrico, peor en ayunas o nocturno.
Pérdida de apetito y pérdida de peso.
Hematemesis o melena en casos de sangrado.
diagnostics: Prueba de aliento con urea (positiva para H. pylori).
Serología o antígeno en heces para H. pylori.
Endoscopia digestiva alta con biopsia para confirmar úlcera y descartar malignidad.
Hemograma: Hb <12 g/dL sugiere sangrado oculto.
treatment: Inhibidor de la bomba de protones (p. ej., omeprazol, pantoprazol).
Bloqueador H2 (ranitidina, famotidina) si PPI no está disponible.
Terapia triple para H. pylori: claritromicina + amoxicilina + PPI (14 días).
Suspender AINE y evitar irritantes (café, alcohol, tabaco).
complications: Obstrucción gástrica por edema o cicatrización.
nursing_care: Evaluar dolor usando escala numérica cada 4 h.
Monitorear signos vitales y hemoglobina cada 24 h si hay sangrado.
Verificar ingesta de alimentos y tolerancia a la dieta blanda.
Administrar PPI según orden y observar efectos adversos (cefalea, diarrea).
Mantener reposo relativo y posición semisentada para reducir irritación.
patient_teaching: Tomar los medicamentos exactamente como se indica, sin omitir dosis.
Evitar AINE, alcohol, tabaco y comidas muy picantes.
Seguir dieta blanda: evitar café, cítricos y chocolate.
Reportar sangrado (vómito con sangre o heces negras) inmediatamente.
Completar el esquema antibiótico aunque los síntomas mejoren.

evidenced_by: dolor epigástrico que empeora entre comidas
outcomes: Paciente reporta disminución del malestar al ingerir alimentos

interventions.action: Evaluar dolor con escala numérica cada 4 h y registrar cambios.
interventions.rationale: Permite medir la efectividad del tratamiento y ajustar la terapia.

interventions.action: Administrar inhibidor de bomba de protones según prescripción y observar efectos adversos.
interventions.rationale: Reduce la secreción ácida y favorece la cicatrización de la úlcera.

interventions.action: Ofrecer alimentos blandos y fraccionados cada 2‑3 h.
interventions.rationale: Minimiza la irritación gástrica y mejora la tolerancia al alimento.

interventions.action: Enseñar al paciente técnicas de relajación y respiración profunda.
interventions.rationale: Disminuye la percepción del dolor y el estrés asociado.

care_plans.diagnosis: Riesgo de déficit de volumen de líquidos
outcomes: Hemoglobina estable o sin descenso >1 g/dL en 48 h

interventions.action: Monitorear signos vitales y nivel de conciencia cada 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Detecta precozmente signos de hipovolemia o shock.

interventions.action: Registrar ingesta y eliminación de líquidos; comparar con balance esperado.
interventions.rationale: Identifica déficit de volumen y guía reposición hídrica.

interventions.action: Administrar solución salina isotónica si hay evidencia de pérdida de sangre o deshidratación.
interventions.rationale: Restablece el volumen intravascular y previene hipotensión.

interventions.action: Observar orina: color claro y volumen ≥30 mL/h.
Educar al paciente sobre la importancia de reportar vómitos con sangre o melena.
interventions.rationale: Facilita la detección temprana de sangrado y permite intervención rápida.

en.summary: Erosive lesion of the gastric or duodenal mucosa primarily caused by H. pylori or chronic NSAIDs.
key_points: Epigastric pain worsens between meals and improves with food or antacids.
H. pylori and NSAIDs are the most common risk factors.
Diagnosis: breath test/serology/heme culture and endoscopy with biopsy.
Treatment: proton pump inhibitors + antibiotic therapy if H. pylori present.

pathophysiology: Gastric acid damages the mucosa when the protective barrier is compromised.
H. pylori produces urease that neutralizes acid and induces chronic inflammation.
NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandins, reducing mucus secretion and mucosal blood flow.
risk_factors: Chronic stress and family history of ulcer.
signs_symptoms: Burning epigastric pain, worse in fasting or at night.
Loss of appetite and weight loss.
Hematemesis or melena in bleeding cases.
diagnostics: Urea breath test (positive for H. pylori).
Serology or fecal antigen for H. pylori.
Upper endoscopy with biopsy to confirm ulcer and rule out malignancy.
CBC: Hb <12 g/dL suggests occult bleeding.
treatment: H2 blocker (ranitidine, famotidine) if PPI unavailable.
Triple therapy for H. pylori: clarithromycin + amoxicillin + PPI (14 days).
Discontinue NSAIDs and avoid irritants (coffee, alcohol, tobacco).
complications: Gastric obstruction from edema or scarring.
nursing_care: Assess pain using numeric scale every 4 h.
Monitor vital signs and hemoglobin every 24 h if bleeding present.
Verify food intake and tolerance to soft diet.
Administer PPI as ordered and observe for adverse effects (headache, diarrhea).
Maintain relative rest and semi‑recumbent position to reduce irritation.
patient_teaching: Take medications exactly as prescribed, do not skip doses.
Avoid NSAIDs, alcohol, tobacco, and very spicy foods.
Follow a soft diet: avoid coffee, citrus, chocolate.
Report bleeding (vomiting blood or black stools) immediately.
Complete the antibiotic course even if symptoms improve.

outcomes: Pain controlled: numeric scale ≤3/10 within 48 h
Patient reports decreased discomfort after eating

interventions.action: Assess pain with numeric scale every 4 h and record changes.
interventions.rationale: Allows measurement of treatment effectiveness and therapy adjustment.

interventions.action: Administer proton pump inhibitor as prescribed and monitor for adverse effects.
interventions.rationale: Reduces acid secretion and promotes ulcer healing.

interventions.action: Offer small, frequent meals every 2‑3 h.
interventions.rationale: Minimizes gastric irritation and improves food tolerance.

interventions.action: Teach patient relaxation and deep‑breathing techniques.
interventions.rationale: Reduces pain perception and associated stress.

outcomes: Stable hemoglobin or no drop >1 g/dL in 48 h

interventions.action: Monitor vital signs and level of consciousness every 4 h.
interventions.rationale: Detects early signs of hypovolemia or shock.

interventions.action: Record fluid intake and output; compare with expected balance.
interventions.rationale: Identifies volume deficit and guides fluid replacement.

interventions.action: Administer isotonic saline if evidence of blood loss or dehydration.
interventions.rationale: Restores intravascular volume and prevents hypotension.

interventions.action: Observe urine: clear color and output ≥30 mL/h.
Educate patient on importance of reporting vomiting with blood or melena.
interventions.rationale: Facilitates early detection of bleeding and allows prompt intervention.

summary.1.quote: The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori . Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen.

key_points.0.quote: The pain: Starts between meals or during the night Briefly stops if you eat or take antacids Lasts for minutes to hours Comes and goes for several days or weeks

key_points.1.quote: The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori . Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen.

key_points.3.quote: Treatment may include medicines to reduce stomach acids or antibiotics to kill H. pylori.

sections.pathophysiology.0.quote: Famotidine reduces the output of hydrochloric acid from the parietal cells, which in turn reduces the erosive damage to the gastric mucosa that may occur from hyperacidity.

sections.risk_factors.0.quote: The most common cause is infection with a bacterium called Helicobacter pylori .

sections.risk_factors.1.quote: Another cause is the long-term use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) such as aspirin and ibuprofen.

sections.risk_factors.2.quote: Not smoking and avoiding alcohol can help.

sections.signs_symptoms.0.quote: A burning stomach pain is the most common symptom.

sections.diagnostics.0.quote: To see if you have an H. pylori infection, your doctor will test your blood, breath, or stool.

sections.treatment.0.quote: Pantoprazole suppresses gastric acid production by inhibiting the proton pump in the parietal cells.

sections.treatment.3.quote: “While I am taking this medication I will avoid alcohol, spicy foods, and ibuprofen.”

sections.nursing_care.3.quote: Typical adverse effects include headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and cough.

sections.patient_teaching.0.quote: Adhere to dosing regimen as prescribed by the health care provider, typically short-term administration of 4–8 weeks.
